title: SDK projects, LangVersion, implicit usings
hook: The `.csproj` is the build contract: SDK, TFM, and usually the C# version. Pinning `LangVersion` to `latest` is how CI boxes disagree.

sections.heading: SDK-style project and language version
sections.prose: Modern apps use an SDK-style project: `<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">` plus `<TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>`. The TFM selects the default C# version — .NET 10 means C# 14 unless you override. Visual Studio hides a language-version dropdown because the supported pairing is TFM-driven: a newer LangVersion than the TFM is unsupported. If you must override, set `<LangVersion>14.0</LangVersion>` (or `preview`) in the csproj or `Directory.Build.props`. Do not use `latest`; it means “whatever compiler is installed,” so two build agents can accept different syntax. Dump the actual pair with `#error version` in a file — the compiler replies with compiler and language versions.

snippets.label: Wrong vs right LangVersion
snippets.code:
<!-- Wrong: machine-dependent syntax -->
<LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>

<!-- Right: TFM implies C# 14 on net10.0; override only when you mean it -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
snippets.explanation: net10.0 + current SDK already compiles as C# 14. Explicit latest makes builds non-reproducible across SDK installs.

sections.heading: Implicit usings
sections.prose: `<ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>` injects a generated `global using` set (`System`, `System.Collections.Generic`, `System.Linq`, `System.Threading.Tasks`, and more depending on SDK). That is why a new console app can call `Console.WriteLine` and `List<T>` with no `using`. It is project sugar, not a language keyword that “imports the world.” Disable it in a library if you want every dependency visible in source — common in shared CSV-import utilities that should not accidentally pull `System.Net.Http`.

interviewTakeaways: Default language version follows the target framework; .NET 10 maps to C# 14.
`LangVersion=latest` is a reproducibility smell; prefer TFM or an explicit major like `14.0`.
Implicit usings are generated global usings, not magic scope.
commonPitfalls: Raising LangVersion without raising TFM, then hitting missing runtime APIs.
Thinking implicit usings replace NuGet references — they only import namespaces already referenced by the SDK.
Copy-pasting `Directory.Build.props` LangVersion across C# and VB projects — the version numbers are not the same language.

jsTsCorrelations.note: `compilerOptions.target` and `lib` are closer to TFM than to LangVersion. `latest` in tsconfig is similarly a “depends which tsc” risk.
